Lines in space

Vector equation

r=r0+t d\mathbf r = \mathbf r_0 + t\,\mathbf dr=r0​+tdt∈Rt \in \mathbb Rt∈R

r0=(x0,y0,z0)\mathbf r_0 = (x_0, y_0, z_0)r0​=(x0​,y0​,z0​) a point, d=(a,b,c)\mathbf d = (a, b, c)d=(a,b,c) a direction vector.

The idea

A line is fixed by one point P0P_0P0​ and one direction d\mathbf dd. Start at P0P_0P0​ and walk ttt times the vector d\mathbf dd: every real ttt gives one point of the line, t=0t = 0t=0 gives P0P_0P0​, negative ttt walks backwards.

Worked example

Line through A(1,0,2)A(1, 0, 2)A(1,0,2) with direction (2,1,−1)(2, 1, -1)(2,1,−1). Putting t=2t = 2t=2 gives the point (5,2,0)(5, 2, 0)(5,2,0). To test whether B(−1,−1,3)B(-1, -1, 3)B(−1,−1,3) is on the line, look for one ttt that works in all three coordinates: t=−1t = -1t=−1 does.

Parametric equations

x=x0+at,y=y0+bt,z=z0+ctx = x_0 + at, \quad y = y_0 + bt, \quad z = z_0 + ctx=x0​+at,y=y0​+bt,z=z0​+ct

Symbols: (x0,y0,z0)(x_0, y_0, z_0)(x0​,y0​,z0​): a point of the line, (a,b,c)(a, b, c)(a,b,c): a direction vector, ttt: the parameter.

The idea

Write the vector equation coordinate by coordinate: three equations that share the same parameter ttt. The numbers in front of ttt form the direction; the constant terms are the point at t=0t = 0t=0.

Worked example

From r=(1,−2,0)+t (3,1,2)\mathbf r = (1, -2, 0) + t\,(3, 1, 2)r=(1,−2,0)+t(3,1,2) read x=1+3tx = 1 + 3tx=1+3t, y=−2+ty = -2 + ty=−2+t, z=2tz = 2tz=2t. Which point has x=7x = 7x=7? The first equation gives t=2t = 2t=2; the other two then give y=0y = 0y=0, z=4z = 4z=4.

Symmetric (continuous) form

x−x0a=y−y0b=z−z0c\frac{x - x_0}{a} = \frac{y - y_0}{b} = \frac{z - z_0}{c}ax−x0​​=by−y0​​=cz−z0​​

The idea

Solve each parametric equation for ttt and set the three results equal. You can read the point (the numbers subtracted) and the direction (the denominators) at a glance. If a component of d\mathbf dd is 0, that coordinate is constant and is written apart, e.g. z=2z = 2z=2.

Worked example

For x−12=y+3−1=z4\frac{x - 1}{2} = \frac{y + 3}{-1} = \frac z42x−1​=−1y+3​=4z​: the point is (1,−3,0)(1, -3, 0)(1,−3,0) (watch the sign: y+3=y−(−3)y + 3 = y - (-3)y+3=y−(−3)) and the direction is (2,−1,4)(2, -1, 4)(2,−1,4). Calling the common value ttt gives back the parametric form.

Through two points

d=P2−P1\mathbf d = P_2 - P_1d=P2​−P1​r=P1+t (P2−P1)\mathbf r = P_1 + t\,(P_2 - P_1)r=P1​+t(P2​−P1​)

Symbols: P1P_1P1​, P2P_2P2​: the two points; d\mathbf dd: the direction vector.

The idea

Two points fix a line. The vector from P1P_1P1​ to P2P_2P2​ is a direction, and either point can be the starting point. Then t=0t = 0t=0 is P1P_1P1​, t=1t = 1t=1 is P2P_2P2​, and t=12t = \tfrac12t=21​ is the midpoint.

Worked example

For A(1,2,0)A(1, 2, 0)A(1,2,0) and B(3,1,4)B(3, 1, 4)B(3,1,4): d=B−A=(2,−1,4)\mathbf d = B - A = (2, -1, 4)d=B−A=(2,−1,4), so r=(1,2,0)+t (2,−1,4)\mathbf r = (1, 2, 0) + t\,(2, -1, 4)r=(1,2,0)+t(2,−1,4). Check: t=1t = 1t=1 gives BBB. The midpoint is t=12t = \tfrac12t=21​: (2,32,2)(2, \tfrac32, 2)(2,23​,2).

A(1,2,0)A(1, 2, 0)A(1,2,0), B(3,1,4)B(3, 1, 4)B(3,1,4): d=(2,−1,4)\mathbf d = (2, -1, 4)d=(2,−1,4), r=(1,2,0)+t (2,−1,4)\mathbf r = (1, 2, 0) + t\,(2, -1, 4)r=(1,2,0)+t(2,−1,4).

As two planes

{A1x+B1y+C1z=D1A2x+B2y+C2z=D2\begin{cases} A_1x + B_1y + C_1z = D_1\\ A_2x + B_2y + C_2z = D_2\end{cases}{A1​x+B1​y+C1​z=D1​A2​x+B2​y+C2​z=D2​​d=n1×n2\mathbf d = \mathbf n_1 \times \mathbf n_2d=n1​×n2​

Symbols: n1\mathbf n_1n1​, n2\mathbf n_2n2​: the normal vectors of the two planes; ×\times×: cross product.

The idea

Two non-parallel planes meet in a line. The line lies in both planes, so its direction is perpendicular to both normals: the cross product n1×n2\mathbf n_1\times\mathbf n_2n1​×n2​ gives it. For a point, fix one coordinate (often z=0z = 0z=0) and solve the two equations.

Worked example

For x+y+z=6x + y + z = 6x+y+z=6 and x−y+2z=5x - y + 2z = 5x−y+2z=5: n1×n2=(1,1,1)×(1,−1,2)=(3,−1,−2)\mathbf n_1\times\mathbf n_2 = (1, 1, 1)\times(1, -1, 2) = (3, -1, -2)n1​×n2​=(1,1,1)×(1,−1,2)=(3,−1,−2). With z=0z = 0z=0: x+y=6x + y = 6x+y=6 and x−y=5x - y = 5x−y=5, so x=112x = \tfrac{11}2x=211​, y=12y = \tfrac12y=21​.

x+y+z=3x + y + z = 3x+y+z=3, x−y=1x - y = 1x−y=1: d=(1,1,−2)\mathbf d = (1, 1, -2)d=(1,1,−2); z=0z = 0z=0 gives the point (2,1,0)(2, 1, 0)(2,1,0).

Planes

Normal form

n⋅(r−r0)=0\mathbf n\cdot(\mathbf r - \mathbf r_0) = 0n⋅(r−r0​)=0A(x−x0)+B(y−y0)+C(z−z0)=0A(x - x_0) + B(y - y_0) + C(z - z_0) = 0A(x−x0​)+B(y−y0​)+C(z−z0​)=0

Symbols: n=(A,B,C)\mathbf n = (A, B, C)n=(A,B,C): a normal vector (perpendicular to the plane); r0=(x0,y0,z0)\mathbf r_0 = (x_0, y_0, z_0)r0​=(x0​,y0​,z0​): a point of it.

The idea

A plane is fixed by one point P0P_0P0​ and a normal vector n\mathbf nn perpendicular to it. A point PPP is in the plane exactly when the vector P−P0P - P_0P−P0​ lies flat in the plane, i.e. is perpendicular to n\mathbf nn: the dot product is 0.

Worked example

Plane through (1,2,3)(1, 2, 3)(1,2,3) with normal (2,−1,1)(2, -1, 1)(2,−1,1): 2(x−1)−(y−2)+(z−3)=02(x - 1) - (y - 2) + (z - 3) = 02(x−1)−(y−2)+(z−3)=0. Expanding gives 2x−y+z−3=02x - y + z - 3 = 02x−y+z−3=0. Check with the point: 2−2+3−3=02 - 2 + 3 - 3 = 02−2+3−3=0.

General equation

Ax+By+Cz+D=0Ax + By + Cz + D = 0Ax+By+Cz+D=0n=(A,B,C)\mathbf n = (A, B, C)n=(A,B,C)

The idea

Expand the normal form and every plane becomes Ax+By+Cz+D=0Ax + By + Cz + D = 0Ax+By+Cz+D=0. Read it backwards: the coefficients of x,y,zx, y, zx,y,z are a normal vector, and a point is on the plane when it makes the left side 0. Parallel planes share A,B,CA, B, CA,B,C and differ only in DDD.

Worked example

In 2x+y−2z+4=02x + y - 2z + 4 = 02x+y−2z+4=0 the normal is (2,1,−2)(2, 1, -2)(2,1,−2), of length 333. Is (1,0,3)(1, 0, 3)(1,0,3) on it? 2+0−6+4=02 + 0 - 6 + 4 = 02+0−6+4=0: yes. The point (0,0,0)(0, 0, 0)(0,0,0) gives 4≠04 \ne 04=0: not on it.

Parametric form

r=r0+s u+t v\mathbf r = \mathbf r_0 + s\,\mathbf u + t\,\mathbf vr=r0​+su+tvn=u×v\mathbf n = \mathbf u \times \mathbf vn=u×v

Symbols: u\mathbf uu, v\mathbf vv: two non-parallel direction vectors in the plane; sss, ttt: parameters.

The idea

From a point, two non-parallel vectors u,v\mathbf u, \mathbf vu,v lying in the plane reach every point: two parameters s,ts, ts,t. To turn it into an equation, take n=u×v\mathbf n = \mathbf u\times\mathbf vn=u×v (perpendicular to both) and use the normal form.

Worked example

r=(1,0,0)+s (1,1,0)+t (0,1,2)\mathbf r = (1, 0, 0) + s\,(1, 1, 0) + t\,(0, 1, 2)r=(1,0,0)+s(1,1,0)+t(0,1,2). The normal is (1,1,0)×(0,1,2)=(2,−2,1)(1, 1, 0)\times(0, 1, 2) = (2, -2, 1)(1,1,0)×(0,1,2)=(2,−2,1), so 2(x−1)−2y+z=02(x - 1) - 2y + z = 02(x−1)−2y+z=0, that is 2x−2y+z−2=02x - 2y + z - 2 = 02x−2y+z−2=0.

Through three points

n=(P2−P1)×(P3−P1)\mathbf n = (P_2 - P_1)\times(P_3 - P_1)n=(P2​−P1​)×(P3​−P1​)∣x−x1y−y1z−z1x2−x1y2−y1z2−z1x3−x1y3−y1z3−z1∣=0\begin{vmatrix} x - x_1 & y - y_1 & z - z_1\\ x_2 - x_1 & y_2 - y_1 & z_2 - z_1\\ x_3 - x_1 & y_3 - y_1 & z_3 - z_1\end{vmatrix} = 0​x−x1​x2​−x1​x3​−x1​​y−y1​y2​−y1​y3​−y1​​z−z1​z2​−z1​z3​−z1​​​=0

Symbols: P1P_1P1​, P2P_2P2​, P3P_3P3​: three points not on one line, Pi=(xi,yi,zi)P_i = (x_i, y_i, z_i)Pi​=(xi​,yi​,zi​).

The idea

Three points not on one line fix a plane. The vectors P1P2P_1P_2P1​P2​ and P1P3P_1P_3P1​P3​ lie in it, so their cross product is a normal. Then use the normal form with P1P_1P1​, and check the other two points — a quick way to catch sign slips.

Worked example

A(1,0,0)A(1, 0, 0)A(1,0,0), B(0,2,0)B(0, 2, 0)B(0,2,0), C(0,0,3)C(0, 0, 3)C(0,0,3): AB→=(−1,2,0)\overrightarrow{AB} = (-1, 2, 0)AB=(−1,2,0), AC→=(−1,0,3)\overrightarrow{AC} = (-1, 0, 3)AC=(−1,0,3), and their cross product is (6,3,2)(6, 3, 2)(6,3,2). The plane is 6(x−1)+3y+2z=06(x - 1) + 3y + 2z = 06(x−1)+3y+2z=0, i.e. 6x+3y+2z=66x + 3y + 2z = 66x+3y+2z=6. Check BBB: 6=66 = 66=6; check CCC: 6=66 = 66=6.

(1,0,0)(1, 0, 0)(1,0,0), (0,2,0)(0, 2, 0)(0,2,0), (0,0,3)(0, 0, 3)(0,0,3): n=(−1,2,0)×(−1,0,3)=(6,3,2)\mathbf n = (-1, 2, 0)\times(-1, 0, 3) = (6, 3, 2)n=(−1,2,0)×(−1,0,3)=(6,3,2), so 6x+3y+2z=66x + 3y + 2z = 66x+3y+2z=6.

Intercept form

xa+yb+zc=1\frac xa + \frac yb + \frac zc = 1ax​+by​+cz​=1

Cuts the axes at (a,0,0)(a, 0, 0)(a,0,0), (0,b,0)(0, b, 0)(0,b,0), (0,0,c)(0, 0, c)(0,0,c).

The idea

If a plane cuts the axes at (a,0,0)(a, 0, 0)(a,0,0), (0,b,0)(0, b, 0)(0,b,0) and (0,0,c)(0, 0, c)(0,0,c), its equation is xa+yb+zc=1\frac xa + \frac yb + \frac zc = 1ax​+by​+cz​=1: put each point in and only one fraction survives, equal to 1. Backwards, divide Ax+By+Cz=KAx + By + Cz = KAx+By+Cz=K by KKK to read the intercepts. The plane cuts off a tetrahedron of volume abc6\tfrac{abc}{6}6abc​.

Worked example

x2+y3+z6=1\frac x2 + \frac y3 + \frac z6 = 12x​+3y​+6z​=1 cuts the axes at 2, 3 and 6. Multiply by 6 to clear fractions: 3x+2y+z=63x + 2y + z = 63x+2y+z=6. The tetrahedron it cuts off has volume 2⋅3⋅66=6\tfrac{2\cdot 3\cdot 6}{6} = 662⋅3⋅6​=6.

3x+2y+z=63x + 2y + z = 63x+2y+z=6 divided by 6: x2+y3+z6=1\frac x2 + \frac y3 + \frac z6 = 12x​+3y​+6z​=1; the tetrahedron has volume 2⋅3⋅66=6\frac{2\cdot 3\cdot 6}{6} = 662⋅3⋅6​=6.

Coordinate planes

xy: z=0xy:\ z = 0xy: z=0yz: x=0yz:\ x = 0yz: x=0xz: y=0xz:\ y = 0xz: y=0

The idea

The three coordinate planes are where one coordinate is 0: z=0z = 0z=0 is the floor (xyxyxy-plane), x=0x = 0x=0 and y=0y = 0y=0 are the two walls. A plane z=kz = kz=k is parallel to the floor. The distance from a point to a coordinate plane is just the absolute value of the missing coordinate.

Worked example

For P(2,−1,3)P(2, -1, 3)P(2,−1,3): dropping it onto the xyxyxy-plane gives (2,−1,0)(2, -1, 0)(2,−1,0), its distance to the xzxzxz-plane is ∣−1∣=1\lvert -1\rvert = 1∣−1∣=1, and its mirror image in the xyxyxy-plane is (2,−1,−3)(2, -1, -3)(2,−1,−3) — only the sign of zzz changes.

Angles

Two lines

cos⁡θ=∣d1⋅d2∣∣d1∣ ∣d2∣\cos\theta = \frac{|\mathbf d_1\cdot\mathbf d_2|}{|\mathbf d_1|\,|\mathbf d_2|}cosθ=∣d1​∣∣d2​∣∣d1​⋅d2​∣​

Symbols: d1\mathbf d_1d1​, d2\mathbf d_2d2​: direction vectors of the lines; θ\thetaθ: the angle between them.

The idea

The angle between two lines is the angle between their direction vectors — even when the lines are skew and never meet. The absolute value picks the acute angle: a line has no arrow, so θ\thetaθ and 180∘−θ180^\circ - \theta180∘−θ describe the same pair.

Worked example

For directions (1,1,0)(1, 1, 0)(1,1,0) and (1,0,1)(1, 0, 1)(1,0,1): the dot product is 111, each length is 2\sqrt22​, so cos⁡θ=12\cos\theta = \tfrac12cosθ=21​ and θ=60∘\theta = 60^\circθ=60∘.

Explain it step by step on the blackboard →

Two planes

cos⁡θ=∣n1⋅n2∣∣n1∣ ∣n2∣\cos\theta = \frac{|\mathbf n_1\cdot\mathbf n_2|}{|\mathbf n_1|\,|\mathbf n_2|}cosθ=∣n1​∣∣n2​∣∣n1​⋅n2​∣​

Symbols: n1\mathbf n_1n1​, n2\mathbf n_2n2​: the normal vectors of the planes.

The idea

Two planes meet at the same angle as their normal vectors (turn the picture: tilting one plane tilts its normal by the same amount). Again the absolute value gives the acute angle; n1⋅n2=0\mathbf n_1\cdot\mathbf n_2 = 0n1​⋅n2​=0 means perpendicular planes.

Worked example

Planes 2x+y+2z=52x + y + 2z = 52x+y+2z=5 and z=0z = 0z=0: normals (2,1,2)(2, 1, 2)(2,1,2) and (0,0,1)(0, 0, 1)(0,0,1). Dot product 222, lengths 333 and 111: cos⁡θ=23\cos\theta = \tfrac23cosθ=32​, so θ≈48.19∘\theta \approx 48.19^\circθ≈48.19∘.

2x+y+2z=52x + y + 2z = 52x+y+2z=5 and z=0z = 0z=0: cos⁡θ=23⋅1\cos\theta = \frac{2}{3\cdot 1}cosθ=3⋅12​, θ≈48.2∘\theta \approx 48.2^\circθ≈48.2∘.

Line and plane

sin⁡θ=∣d⋅n∣∣d∣ ∣n∣\sin\theta = \frac{|\mathbf d\cdot\mathbf n|}{|\mathbf d|\,|\mathbf n|}sinθ=∣d∣∣n∣∣d⋅n∣​

Sine, not cosine: the angle with the normal is 90∘−θ90^\circ - \theta90∘−θ.

Symbols: d\mathbf dd: direction of the line, n\mathbf nn: normal of the plane.

The idea

The angle between a line and a plane is measured against the plane, but the formula uses the normal. The angle between d\mathbf dd and n\mathbf nn is 90∘−θ90^\circ - \theta90∘−θ, and cos⁡(90∘−θ)=sin⁡θ\cos(90^\circ - \theta) = \sin\thetacos(90∘−θ)=sinθ: that is why this formula has a sine. A line parallel to the plane gives d⋅n=0\mathbf d\cdot\mathbf n = 0d⋅n=0.

Worked example

Direction (1,0,1)(1, 0, 1)(1,0,1) and the plane z=0z = 0z=0 with normal (0,0,1)(0, 0, 1)(0,0,1): d⋅n=1\mathbf d\cdot\mathbf n = 1d⋅n=1, lengths 2\sqrt22​ and 111, so sin⁡θ=12\sin\theta = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}sinθ=2​1​ and θ=45∘\theta = 45^\circθ=45∘.

d=(1,0,1)\mathbf d = (1, 0, 1)d=(1,0,1) and z=0z = 0z=0: sin⁡θ=12\sin\theta = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}sinθ=2​1​, so θ=45∘\theta = 45^\circθ=45∘.

Distances

Point to plane

d=∣Ax0+By0+Cz0+D∣A2+B2+C2d = \frac{|Ax_0 + By_0 + Cz_0 + D|}{\sqrt{A^2 + B^2 + C^2}}d=A2+B2+C2​∣Ax0​+By0​+Cz0​+D∣​

Symbols: (x0,y0,z0)(x_0, y_0, z_0)(x0​,y0​,z0​): the point; Ax+By+Cz+D=0Ax + By + Cz + D = 0Ax+By+Cz+D=0: the plane.

The idea

Plug the point into the left side of the plane’s equation: the result is 0 on the plane and grows as you move away along the normal. Dividing by ∣n∣\lvert\mathbf n\rvert∣n∣ turns it into a true distance; the absolute value removes the side.

Worked example

From P(1,2,3)P(1, 2, 3)P(1,2,3) to 2x−y+2z+4=02x - y + 2z + 4 = 02x−y+2z+4=0: the left side gives 2−2+6+4=102 - 2 + 6 + 4 = 102−2+6+4=10 and ∣n∣=4+1+4=3\lvert\mathbf n\rvert = \sqrt{4 + 1 + 4} = 3∣n∣=4+1+4​=3, so d=103d = \tfrac{10}{3}d=310​.

P(1,2,3)P(1, 2, 3)P(1,2,3) and 2x−y+2z+4=02x - y + 2z + 4 = 02x−y+2z+4=0: d=∣2−2+6+4∣3=103d = \frac{\lvert 2 - 2 + 6 + 4\rvert}{3} = \frac{10}{3}d=3∣2−2+6+4∣​=310​.

Point to line

d=∣P0Q→×d∣∣d∣d = \frac{\left|\overrightarrow{P_0Q}\times\mathbf d\right|}{|\mathbf d|}d=∣d∣​P0​Q​×d​​

P0P_0P0​ on the line, QQQ the point.

The idea

∣P0Q→×d∣\lvert\overrightarrow{P_0Q}\times\mathbf d\rvert∣P0​Q​×d∣ is the area of the parallelogram built on P0Q→\overrightarrow{P_0Q}P0​Q​ and d\mathbf dd. Its base is ∣d∣\lvert\mathbf d\rvert∣d∣ and its height is exactly the distance from QQQ to the line, so area ÷ base = distance.

Worked example

Q(3,0,0)Q(3, 0, 0)Q(3,0,0) and the line (1,0,1)+t (1,1,0)(1, 0, 1) + t\,(1, 1, 0)(1,0,1)+t(1,1,0): P0Q→=(2,0,−1)\overrightarrow{P_0Q} = (2, 0, -1)P0​Q​=(2,0,−1), its cross product with d\mathbf dd is (1,−1,2)(1, -1, 2)(1,−1,2) of length 6\sqrt66​, and ∣d∣=2\lvert\mathbf d\rvert = \sqrt2∣d∣=2​. So d=6/2=3d = \sqrt6/\sqrt2 = \sqrt3d=6​/2​=3​.

Skew lines

d=∣P1P2→⋅(d1×d2)∣∣d1×d2∣d = \frac{\left|\overrightarrow{P_1P_2}\cdot(\mathbf d_1\times\mathbf d_2)\right|}{|\mathbf d_1\times\mathbf d_2|}d=∣d1​×d2​∣​P1​P2​​⋅(d1​×d2​)​​

Symbols: P1P_1P1​, P2P_2P2​: one point on each line; d1\mathbf d_1d1​, d2\mathbf d_2d2​: their directions.

The idea

Skew lines are neither parallel nor meeting. d1×d2\mathbf d_1\times\mathbf d_2d1​×d2​ is perpendicular to both, the direction of their common perpendicular. The distance is the length of the shadow of P1P2→\overrightarrow{P_1P_2}P1​P2​​ on that direction: dot product, divided by the length.

Worked example

Substitute the parametric line into the plane. If n⋅d=0\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf d = 0n⋅d=0 the line is parallel to the plane (or lies in it).

The idea

Every point of the line is r0+t d\mathbf r_0 + t\,\mathbf dr0​+td. Put that into the plane’s equation: it becomes one equation in ttt. Solve it and put ttt back into the line. det⁡(A1B1C1A2B2C2A3B3C3)≠0 ⇒ ∃! P\det\begin{pmatrix}A_1 & B_1 & C_1\\ A_2 & B_2 & C_2\\ A_3 & B_3 & C_3\end{pmatrix} \ne 0 \ \Rightarrow\ \exists!\,Pdet​A1​A2​A3​​B1​B2​B3​​C1​C2​C3​​​=0 ⇒ ∃!P

Exactly one common point; solve the system (Cramer). Otherwise they share a line, or nothing.

The idea

Three planes are a 3×3 linear system. If the determinant of the normals is not 0 the three normals point in independent directions and the planes share exactly one point. If it is 0 they share a whole line, or nothing at all (like the three faces of a prism).

Worked example

x+y+z=6x + y + z = 6x+y+z=6, x−y+z=2x - y + z = 2x−y+z=2, x+y−z=0x + y - z = 0x+y−z=0. Subtracting the second from the first: 2y=42y = 42y=4, y=2y = 2y=2. Subtracting the third from the first: 2z=62z = 62z=6, z=3z = 3z=3. Then x=1x = 1x=1. The single common point is (1,2,3)(1, 2, 3)(1,2,3) (the determinant is 4≠04 \ne 04=0).

Equation

The idea

A sphere is every point at distance rrr from the centre C(a,b,c)C(a, b, c)C(a,b,c). Write that distance with Pythagoras in 3D and square it to remove the root. To test a point, plug it in: less than r2r^2r2 inside, equal on the sphere, more outside.

Centre (1,−2,3)(1, -2, 3)(1,−2,3) and radius 4: (x−1)2+(y+2)2+(z−3)2=16(x - 1)^2 + (y + 2)^2 + (z - 3)^2 = 16(x−1)2+(y+2)2+(z−3)2=16. Is (1,2,3)(1, 2, 3)(1,2,3) on it? 0+16+0=160 + 16 + 0 = 160+16+0=16: yes. And (2,0,4)(2, 0, 4)(2,0,4)? 1+4+1=6<161 + 4 + 1 = 6 < 161+4+1=6<16: inside.

The tangent plane at a point TTT of the sphere is perpendicular to the radius CTCTCT. So CT→\overrightarrow{CT}CT is its normal and TTT is one of its points: just the normal form. The card’s formula is the same thing, written to look like the sphere’s equation.

Worked example

Sphere x2+y2+z2=9x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 9x2+y2+z2=9 at T(1,2,2)T(1, 2, 2)T(1,2,2) (on it: 1+4+4=91 + 4 + 4 = 91+4+4=9). The normal is OT→=(1,2,2)\overrightarrow{OT} = (1, 2, 2)OT=(1,2,2), so 1(x−1)+2(y−2)+2(z−2)=01(x - 1) + 2(y - 2) + 2(z - 2) = 01(x−1)+2(y−2)+2(z−2)=0, i.e. x+2y+2z=9x + 2y + 2z = 9x+2y+2z=9.
